newsitem.title: USA: CSCE defends plan to halve size of coffee contract.
newsitem.headline: CSCE defends plan to halve size of coffee contract.

text.p: The Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange (CSCE), responding to complaints from European traders, defended its proposal to cut the size of its coffee futures contract in half by saying it will boost liquidity.

The European Coffee Federation (ECF) sent a letter to CSCE last month saying it opposed the plan, first broached in April, that will halve the effective trading unit of the coffee "C" contract from about 250 (60-kg) bags to 125 bags.

ECF said the change would create substantial additional costs for futures users because commission had to be paid per transaction. ECF also doubted the plan would help increase market liquidity in an attempt to reduce price volatility.
"We received the letter from the European Coffee Federation and we understand their position," CSCE president James Bowe said in a statement issued by a CSCE spokesman.
Bowe said the 37,500-lb size of the coffee contract was an impediment to trading volume.

"The current dollar value of the coffee contract is far larger than any other agricultural commodity futures contract (at the CSCE) and the exchange coffee committee believes it is possible that the current size may impede liquidity, which is the rationale for the proposal.
"If we can improve the liquidity of the contract, it would be very beneficial to trading," Bowe said. "If we have a more liquid contract, it would more than offset commission cost concerns."

At current prices, the existing spot arabica contract requiring delivery of 37,500 lbs of coffee is worth nearly $69,000. Required trading margins are currently around $6,000 for the spot contract, including a $2,000 spot charge.
CSCE spokesman Terence Gordon said no timetable has been set for the proposed change in the coffee contract, which Bowe made in a speech in April.
The proposal has not been submitted to the CSCE board or the Commodity Futures Trading Commission for approval.
Gordon said current plans, however, were to keep the size of the coffee delivery unit at a nominal 37,500 pounds, requiring two new contracts to fulfill one delivery demand.

The par size of the contract at 37,500 lbs equates to 284 60-kg bags, but actual delivery against the arabica contract averages 250 bags as bag weights vary from different countries of origin, according to CSCE and industry documents.

Brussels-based ECF is the umbrella organization of the European green coffee trade and roasting industry, consisting of national coffee associations in 13 European countries and representing coffee imports of around 36 million bags a year.

In its letter, ECF also stated other concerns with the downsizing of the CSCE contract, such as the delivery basis being limited to only washed arabicas and the inability to deliver coffee spot Europe.
